stories.headline: NFL offseason free agent and trade acquisitions that have and have not worked
stories.summary: Kenneth Walker III and Devin Lloyd look great with their new teams in 2026. But Jaylen Waddle and Alontae Taylor haven't quite found their groove.
stories.body:
Everyone loves the NFL offseason hot stove. Fans get super excited about outside players joining their favorite team, whether through trade or free agency. Those holes on the roster have finally been filled by wily veterans!

Unfortunately, those moves don't always work out. Some players excel in new surroundings, bringing strong production. Others struggle with their new situation, confirming why they were made available in the first place.

Here's a look at five players who are working well with their new teams and five who are not. How are the successful new players helping their teams? Which teams find themselves on the hook for bad contracts? Let's start with a quarterback who has helped two teams this season.

Jump to a section:

Moves that have worked out

Moves that have not yet worked out

Five players who are working

Kirk Cousins, QB, Raiders/Vikings
How he got there: Signed a one-year, $11.3 million contract with the Raiders before being traded to the Vikings on Nov. 10

2026 stat to know: 65.0 QBR (10th out of 31 qualifying QBs)

Comparable 2025 stat: 47.6 QBR (not enough passes to qualify)

This is a bit of a special case, because Cousins is thriving in his second new city of the season. Or perhaps we should say one new and one old city, because Cousins played for Minnesota from 2018 to 2023.

His performance this season is further proof that it takes a long time to recover from an Achilles tear. Cousins tore his Achilles in 2023 on the last play of his previous stint with the Vikings. He went to Atlanta in 2024 and was completely immobile on plays such as rollouts and play-action fakes. He put up a career-low QBR of 47.0 and lost the starting job to then-rookie Michael Penix Jr. toward the end of the season. In 2025, Cousins came in after Penix was hurt and looked a bit better. He was able to avoid turnovers, but his yards per attempt average dropped from 7.7 in 2024 to 6.4. It resulted in his QBR virtually being the same as it was the previous season.

But Cousins is back to being his old self this season. His yards per attempt is up to 7.4, and his 22 passing touchdowns rank second in the NFL. His sack rate of 3.9% is also the lowest of any starting quarterback.

The Raiders were able to get four wins out of Cousins (one more than they earned all last season) until they were ready to transition to rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza. Then they got an additional third-round pick by trading Cousins to Minnesota. Cousins won his first start with the Vikings in Week 10 and dramatically improved their chances of winning the Super Bowl by taking Minnesota's offense from horrific to slightly above average.

Kenneth Walker III, RB, Chiefs
How he got there: Signed a three-year, $43.1 million contract

2026 stat to know: 1.66 rushing yards over expected per attempt (second out of 45 qualifying RBs)

Comparable 2025 stat: 0.25 RYOE/attempt (30th out of 51 qualifying RBs)

Do running backs matter? Well, special running backs are only special when they get enough blocking to do great things. Last season, the Chiefs had the blocking but didn't have a back who could fully take advantage. This season, they have two in Walker and rookie Emmett Johnson.

Walker has always been good at breaking tackles, but he's in another universe this season. According to FTN charting, Walker leads the league with a 35.2% avoided tackle rate and is third with 3.14 yards after contact per carry.

The biggest question about Walker in Kansas City was whether he could handle the workload of a clear No. 1 running back after being in a committee in Seattle. Although Walker missed last week with a groin injury, he's on pace for 318 carries, which would easily exceed his previous career high of 228 set as a rookie in 2022.

Mike Evans, WR, 49ers
How he got there: Signed a three-year, $42.4 million contract

2026 stats to know: minus-12.2% DVOA (63rd out of 79 qualifying WRs), 10.8 yards per target

Comparable 2025 stats: 45.1% DVOA (first out of 58 qualifying WRs), 6.0 yards per target

Evans had a difficult final season in Tampa Bay. Oft-injured QB Baker Mayfield had a hard time getting Evans the ball in places where the receiver could excel. He hit career lows in yards per reception (12.3) and catch rate (48%). Last year was the first season of his career in which he failed to reach 1,000 receiving yards.

Evans has been refreshed and renewed in San Francisco's powerful offense. His catch rate is up to 69%, which would be the highest of his career. He's also averaging 15.6 yards per reception. He had 23 first downs on 62 targets in 2025; this season, he's up to 25 first downs on only 39 targets so far.

The only problem is the Achilles tendinitis that has sidelined Evans since Week 6. The 49ers are being very careful so they can have Evans back and 100 percent for their playoff run. They are hoping he can return in the next couple of weeks and continue to demonstrate why he was such a good signing.

Quincy Williams, LB, Browns
How he got there: Signed a two-year, $13 million contract (up to $17 million with bonuses)

2026 stat to know: Tied for lead among LBs with 20 defeats

Comparable 2025 stat: 15 defeats in 13 games

Williams was a first-team All-Pro for the Jets in 2023 but is still not as well known as his younger brother, Cowboys defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. Quincy had only 12 starts for the Jets last season and turned 30 in August, so it was reasonable to assume that he was at the tail end of his career.

The Browns brought him in on a reasonable contract and stuck him next to Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger, and Williams has been an outstanding playmaker in that role. I keep track of a stat called defeats, which measures defensive splash plays. It combines tackles for loss, turnovers and any play that prevents a third- or fourth-down conversion. Williams has 20 defeats so far this season, tied with the Vikings' Blake Cashman for the lead among all linebackers. (Quinnen leads all players with 24.)

Williams is known for speed and has been excellent in pass coverage, with four passes defensed and 15 pass tackles, which prevented a successful yardage gain despite a reception. Opposing running backs have fewer than 20 receiving yards per game against the Browns.

Devin Lloyd, LB, Panthers
How he got there: Signed a three-year, $42 million contract

2026 stats to know: 16 defeats, three interceptions, average run tackle at 3.3 yards

Comparable 2025 stats: 14 defeats, five interceptions, average run tackle at 4.0 yards

Unlike Williams, Lloyd entered the 2026 season with big expectations. He was one of the NFL's top linebackers last season and signed the largest contract of any free agent off-ball linebacker this past offseason. So far, Lloyd has lived up to that contract.

Entering the season, it was hard to imagine Lloyd getting five interceptions again, but his Week 10 interception already puts him at three. Lloyd already has more defeats than he did last season, too, and he was part of two combined tackles to prevent Saints running back Audric Estime from converting on third-and-short last week. With the NFC South still up for grabs, the Panthers are counting on more big plays from Lloyd to get them back into the postseason.

Five players who are not working

Jaylen Waddle, WR, Broncos
How he got there: Acquired from the Dolphins along with a 2026 fourth-round pick for 2026 first-, third- and fourth-round picks

2026 stat to know: minus-17.6% receiving DVOA (52nd out of 58 qualifying WRs)

Comparable 2025 stat: 11.6% receiving DVOA (19th out of 79 qualifying WRs)

Trading for Waddle was supposed to unlock the Broncos' intermediate passing game and help Bo Nix complete passes over the middle. Instead, Waddle has been victim of Nix's struggles. Right now, Nix ranks 26th in DVOA on passes over the middle and 28th on intermediate passes (10-19 air yards). His numbers in those areas are a little better throwing to Waddle than to other receivers, but they are still not good. Nix is also checking down far too often, another reason Waddle isn't seeing the ball downfield.

An additional issue for Waddle has been injuries, which include a leg injury in training camp and a chest injury in recent weeks that has forced him to be limited in practice. He also left the Week 9 win over the Panthers with a concussion.

Waddle has shown frustration on the field even though the Broncos are winning. The hope is that Nix can do a better job of getting him the ball in the second half of the season, but right now it seems like the Broncos paid a lot of draft value (and took on an expensive contract) for a player their quarterback can't fully utilize.

Cole Strange, G, Chargers
How he got there: Signed a two-year, $13 million contract

2026 stat to know: 77.5% pass block win rate (64th out of 65 qualifying guards)

Comparable 2025 stat: 91.9% pass block win rate (40th out of 65 qualifying guards)

OK, this is less of a surprise. In fact, for many who follow the league, the bigger surprise was that the Chargers signed Strange in the first place. A first-round pick of the Patriots in 2022, Strange lost his job in 2024 and wasn't very good with the Dolphins last season. Was he really an upgrade for a Chargers team that had trouble with its interior offensive line in 2025?

Well, the Chargers are still having interior O-line trouble. Strange is close to the bottom of the league in pass block win rate. He's better in run block win rate but still below average -- 70.7% compared to the league average of 71.3% for guards. You have to imagine the Chargers will be looking for guard help again in 2027.

Chig Okonkwo, TE, Commanders
How he got there: Signed a three-year, $27 million contract

2026 stat to know: minus-20.2% receiving DVOA (37th out of 43 qualifying TEs)

Comparable 2025 stat: minus-11.0% receiving DVOA (43rd out of 55 qualifying TEs)

Okonkwo's performance this season is fully in line with the first four years of his NFL career in Tennessee, but he was supposed to be more than that for the Commanders. There was hope that he could take another step forward at age 27 to become a major part of Washington's passing game. Okonkwo himself told the Commanders' website that "this is the place where I can finally unleash."

It hasn't happened. Okonkwo has never matched the three touchdowns (on only 32 catches) or 14.1 yards per reception he had as a rookie in 2022. He's having another season of reasonable but relatively inefficient production. His 69% catch rate isn't terrible, but it's still below average for tight ends, and the same goes for his average of 9.7 yards per reception. Okonkwo also hasn't found the end zone yet for Washington, but he'll probably end up with a touchdown or two before the season is over. It's just a little disappointing because the Commanders hoped for more.

L'Jarius Sneed, CB, Chiefs
How he got there: Signed a one-year, $1.2 million contract (up to $5 million in incentives)

2026 stat to know: 128.3% coverage DVOA (not enough snaps to qualify but higher is worse)

Comparable 2025 stat: 10.8% coverage DVOA

The Chiefs turned over almost their entire secondary this offseason and have gotten a lot of value out of second-year corner Nohl Williams and first-round rookie Mansoor Delane. But they brought back Sneed, a key player on their back-to-back Super Bowl-winning teams in 2022 and 2023, to play in the slot. That hasn't worked out as well.

With 148 coverage snaps this season, Sneed just misses the line for my coverage DVOA rankings, but he would easily be at the bottom of the league if he qualified. He gave up big play after big play early in the season. In Week 2, he gave up six first downs, plus a goal-line touchdown by Colts tight end Tyler Warren. Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty had a series of 10-yard completions in Sneed's zone that moved the sticks in Week 4. And in Week 7, Sneed got roasted by Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the slot, though he's not the only corner to struggle against JSN.

Sneed went on injured reserve with a knee injury two weeks ago, and it's hard to know if he'll have his previous role in Kansas City's defense back when he returns.

Alontae Taylor, CB, Titans
How he got there: Signed a three-year, $58 million contract

2026 stat to know: 62.2% coverage DVOA (89th out of 89 qualifying CBs)

Comparable 2025 stat: 4.2% coverage DVOA (61st out of 92 qualifying CBs)

The Titans signed Taylor away from the Saints with the idea that they could make him an outside cornerback. It didn't work. Taylor gave up a ton of passes the first few weeks of the season. The nadir was Week 5 against Houston, when Taylor gave up three third-down conversions (including a 9-yard touchdown to Jaylin Noel) and drew a 28-yard pass interference flag.

Taylor was so bad as an outside corner that the Titans benched him. He was a healthy scratch in Week 6 and was active but didn't play in Week 7. He was moved to the slot in Week 8 when nickelback Marcus Harris got hurt and remained there, despite Harris' return in Week 10. But Taylor's play hasn't improved in the slot, as he gave up a couple of long gains to Jaguars receiver Parker Washington last week.

stories.headline: Mikel Arteta: Steps taken to avoid team leaks due to Fantasy Premier League
stories.summary: Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal have taken steps to avoid future team leaks via Fantasy Premier League after Christos Tzolis inadvertently revealed information through his own selections in the game.
stories.body:
Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal have taken steps to avoid future team leaks via Fantasy Premier League after Christos Tzolis inadvertently revealed information through his own selections in the game.

Tzolis selected and captained himself before the Gunners faced Liverpool earlier this month, indicating that he had recovered from a hamstring injury and was in line to start at Anfield.

The following week, Tzolis then transferred himself, Ezri Konsa and Riccardo Calafiori out of his FPL team.

Asked if he had spoken to Tzolis and his teammates about using the game, Arteta said: "With Christos [Tzolis], with the squad, with my kids as well. They are constantly asking me about the line-ups as well because they want to know.

"It's a topic. This is the kind of things that are happening in our society right now and it's something new, we haven't dealt with it and we have to put new things in place.

"But obviously the confidentiality is something critical because it's about trust and what you're trying to do and that should be kept as a huge secret. And we will take measures to make sure that doesn't happen."

Pushed on whether that meant players could no longer select themselves, Arteta replied: "Yeah."

- Mikel Arteta warns of drone breach risk after Man United training incident

- Transfer rumors, news: Arsenal want Athletic's World Cup winner Nico Williams

Arteta's intervention follows on from Chelsea's players and staff being reminded over their FPL use after a number of figures connected to the club transferred out striker João Pedro in October prior to a thigh injury becoming public knowledge.

Arteta confirmed William Saliba is available for the first time this season following a back injury: "He's ready," Arteta said. "He's in a good condition. He played two games, one behind closed doors and one more official and he did really well and he's in good condition. We want to ramp up his minutes."

However, Bukayo Saka is out for another month due to a quad problem and Martín Zubimendi is set to miss "a few weeks" with a hamstring issue sustained in Spain's Nations League defeat to England.

stories.headline: F1 bosses confirm 'agreement' on V8 engine return deal
stories.summary: McLaren CEO Zak Brown has confirmed that an "agreement in principle" exists for Formula 1 to switch to V8 engines, with the final details being worked on ahead of a proposed introduction in 2030.
stories.body:
McLaren CEO Zak Brown has confirmed that an "agreement in principle" exists for Formula 1 to switch to V8 engines, with the final details being worked on ahead of a proposed introduction in 2030.

Brown's comments follow a post on social media by FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem earlier this week that stated: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."

Ben Sulayem's post coincided with what appeared to be an official announcement on the FIA's own social media channels, only for those details to be quickly deleted.

Brown said on Thursday at the Las Vegas Grand Prix that there were still elements to be decided, but that the overarching agreement on V8 engines was in place.

"There's an agreement in principle," he said. "I think everyone is very, very excited. I think now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's."

The plan to introduce the new engine formula was discussed during a meeting of F1, the FIA, teams and power unit manufacturers on Tuesday in London.

Fast-tracking the change for 2030 would see the current engine regulation cycle, which was introduced at the start of this year, cut short by one year.

The existing regulations, which feature 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrids, have been criticised by drivers for being overcomplicated, with four-time champion Max Verstappen labelling the current power units "anti-racing" at the start of the year.

The plan discussed on Tuesday is for F1 to introduce 2.1-litre turbocharged V8s with a less powerful hybrid element than the current power units.

- Antonelli handed grid penalty for Las Vegas GP; Russell sets pace in FP2

- Max Verstappen on F1 retirement, Le Mans and learning to lose: 'Stress a bit less'

- FIA to introduce full-time stewards to address worries over decision-making

The next step is for the final proposal to be agreed upon and presented to the FIA's World Motor Sport Council in Shanghai next month.

Alpine team boss Flavio Briatore said the agreement for 2030 was all but signed.

"We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy," Briatore said. "I think it's the right way to go.

"We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that because, in the end, I believe the best for the spectator, for everybody is a very simple engine, a lot of noise and basta.

"Maybe have some KERS [Kinetic Energy Recovery Systems] or stuff like that, nothing major like we have now."

The current regulations, which require nearly 50% of peak power to come from the power unit's battery, were introduced to keep the sport road-car relevant and entice more engine manufacturers to F1.

In that sense they were successful, with Audi joining this season, Honda returning from the brink of leaving the sport to team up with Aston Martin, and Ford partnering with Red Bull's in-house powertrains department.

However, the emphasis on electric power has proved controversial this year, with drivers forced to change their driving style to manage energy around a lap instead of pushing the cars to the limit.

Two-time champion Fernando Alonso labelled this year's regulations a "battery world championship" following the second race of the season in China, with the sport later agreeing to tweak certain rules to limit the unusual behaviour of the hybrid systems by the fourth round in Miami.

Further changes are planned over the next two seasons to shift the 50/50 split between electrical power and internal combustion engine (ICE) power to 60/40 in favour of the ICE by 2028.

V8 engines were last used in F1 in 2013 and featured a mild hybrid boost known as the Kinetic Energy Recovery System.

The previous era of V8s were known for their evocative exhaust note, but the turbocharged versions proposed for 2030 are not expected to be as loud or high-pitched due to the presence of a turbocharger.

stories.headline: Dike exits wild card loss injured as Orlando's season ends against Cincinnati
stories.summary: FC Cincinnati rallied to eliminate Orlando City 3-1 in MLS Cup Eastern Conference wild card match on Thursday.
stories.body:
Forward Daryl Dike suffered an injury in Orlando City SC's 3-1 defeat to FC Cincinnati in the Major League Soccer playoff wild card match on Thursday night at Inter&Co Stadium in Orlando, Florida.

Dike entered the playoff match in the 75th minute before suffering the injury moments later.

"I don't know what the issue is; we haven't been able to, I haven't had time yet to see the doctors, so I don't know exactly what's wrong," interim coach Martín Perelman said in the post-match press conference.

"I think it's something with his hamstring, since that's where he was holding, so I assume he might have some kind of tear or something similar in the hamstring, but I'm not certain. I don't know exactly what it is, but naturally, he's frustrated, just like the rest of us."

Despite the apparent injury, Dike stayed on the pitch for the rest of the game given that Orlando City did not have any more substitution windows available.

"Regarding the substitutions, these are things that can happen, and they're difficult to predict," Perelman said.

"You never expect a player to come on with 15 minutes left and then get injured; that's not something you anticipate. So, I don't think it's fair to second-guess the substitutions based on that. It simply happened, and that's that-we can't change it now. It was just another piece of misfortune in the match, and, well, as I said, that's part of the game."

Dike has a lengthy injury history, suffering a season-ending hamstring injury in 2022, a right Achilles tendon rupture in 2023, a left Achilles tendon rupture in 2024, and most recently a thigh concern that kept him on the sidelines for 10 matches during the start of the 2025/26 season.

Orlando striker Martín Ojeda opened up the scoring in the 26th minute of the match before goals by Cincinnati players Evander and Samuel Gidi won the game for the visiting side.

Orlando City, in Antoine Griezmann's first season, has now been eliminated from playoff contention.

"We are very disappointed because we wanted to bring happiness to our fans, to our families, and everyone here at the stadium, and we couldn't," said Perelman. "That is frustrating for us, but at the same time, again, the effort was not enough, but it was there. This group of players will bring happiness and achievements to this club."

Cincinnati will now go on to face Nashville SC in the best-of-three round of the playoff series.

stories.headline: Mark Stone becomes Golden Knight's all-time scoring leader in loss to Stars
stories.summary: Mark Stone picked up his 418th point with an assist in Thursday's 4-3 shootout loss to the Stars, becoming the Golden Knights' career scoring leader.
stories.body:
Mark Stone took sole possession of the Vegas Golden Knights' career scoring record Thursday night, picking up his 418th point with an assist in a 4-3 shootout loss to the Dallas Stars.

The Vegas captain set up Victor Olofsson's power-play goal at 7:38 of the second period, cutting Dallas' lead to 2-1 and moving past Jonathan Marchessault on the franchise list. Stone had tied Marchessault with a power-play goal against Vancouver on Sunday.

Stone, 34, has 147 goals and 271 assists with Vegas since arriving in a February 2019 trade with the Ottawa Senators. He finished with 63 points in 2019-20, his first full season with the Golden Knights, and has topped 60 points four times with the club.

Stone matched his career high with 73 points last season, scoring 28 goals and adding 45 assists. He entered Thursday's game with 21 points this season and a team-leading 11 goals.

Having played alongside Stone since arriving in Vegas in 2021, Jack Eichel has seen the captain's ability to influence games beyond what appears on the scoresheet up-close.

"Well, he's a competitor, and he makes a lot of plays, and obviously super smart with the puck and goes to the right areas," Eichel said. "Thinks the game at an elite level and makes a lot of plays."

For Eichel, Stone's ascension to the top of the franchise's scoring list was hardly surprising, considering how instrumental the captain has been to the organization's success.

"Stoney's been here for a while, and he's been leading the charge for a while," Eichel said. "Great, great milestone for him. Happy for him. It's well-earned."

Stone and Marchessault helped Vegas win its first Stanley Cup in 2023. Marchessault won the Conn Smythe Trophy as playoff MVP and finished his seven seasons with the Golden Knights with 192 goals and 225 assists. He joined Vegas for its inaugural season in 2017 and now plays for Nashville.

Vegas followed Olofsson's goal with two more to take a 3-2 lead in the third period, but Dallas tied it with 3:02 left in regulation and handed the Golden Knights their fourth straight home loss.

stories.headline: 2026-27 MLB free agency, trade grades: Offseason analysis
stories.summary: We've got you covered with grades and analysis on every winter signing and big offseason trade.
stories.body:
Hot stove season has finally begun!

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is officially here, and we have you covered with grades and analysis for every major signing and trade as this winter -- which is expected to include a labor stoppage -- unfolds.

Whether it's a franchise-changing free agent signing or an unexpected blockbuster trade, we'll weigh in with what it all means for next season and beyond.

ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle and David Schoenfield will evaluate each move as it happens, so follow along here, as this story will continue to be updated. Check back in for all the most recent analysis.

Related links: Tracker | Top 50 free agents

Rockies add pair of starters in deal with White Sox

Colorado Rockies get:

RHP Davis Martin

RHP Luis Castillo

Chicago White Sox get:

LHP Sean Sullivan

C Douglas Veliz

White Sox grade: C+

The White Sox appear to be spending proverbial money to spend proverbial money. That is to say, they are moving past the Castillo mistake from the last trade deadline -- one whose ramifications were primarily monetary -- and to do it, they are folding in a legitimate starter in Martin -- a pitcher who, for the first few weeks of the 2026 season, looked like a Cy Young candidate. They aren't spending actual money but are rearranging resources in hopes of spending money in a more productive way.

That's just reality, not an attempt to overhype Martin, whose season came unraveled the deeper we got into the calendar and who was ultimately not in position to help Chicago's staff once it reached the postseason. Still, he put up more than 140 innings in each of the past two seasons with a 104 ERA+ during the pre-arbitration phase of his service time window. He was a valuable player for Chicago and therefore is now that for Colorado.

This perspective speaks to how badly the White Sox wanted to clear Castillo off their books, and his departure -- which rids them of a $22.75 million 2027 salary plus a semi-unlikely vesting option for 2028 -- opens up the payroll so that Chicago can further upgrade a rotation it thinks it upgraded with the signing of Dustin May earlier this week.

Castillo was ghastly -- harsh as that sounds -- last season for the Mariners before Chicago acquired him at the trade deadline, and he was even worse after the deal. It was the first truly bad season of his mostly very good 10-year big league career, but it felt like it was one that was a result of trends that were years in the making. The one and truly virtuous aspect of this deal for the White Sox is that it rids them of the considerable risk that Castillo bounces back and justifies his sizable salary.

Sullivan is a long, lean lefty with so-so stuff who relies on deception -- perhaps not the soft-tossing lefty of yore, but someone along those lines. Veliz is a 17-year-old catcher who originally was signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela. Maybe someday you'll read his name again.

Chicago's grade is entirely provisional. The White Sox have opened up payroll space that needs to be parlayed into a meaningful upgrade. The 2027 rotation, once it's in place, will have some kind of configuration that includes May, an unsigned pitcher to be named and the other returnees to the staff. The gamble is that this new group will be better than simply running it back with Castillo while hoping for more consistency from Martin.

Right now, it's hard to say which path would have been better.

Rockies grade: B

I mean, why not? It's easy to make the crude argument against Castillo -- over 126 games for the Mariners, he went 43-40 with a 3.69 ERA while pitching half the time in one of baseball's most pitcher-friendly contexts. (During those seasons, his ERA was 3.07 at T-Mobile Park and 4.38 on the road.) Now he's headed to the wood-chipper of a pitching context at Coors Field and doing so at the nadir of his career.

Still, for the Rockies, it's a worthy gamble especially since it lands them Martin in the process. Is Martin the right pitcher for Coors Field? Who knows? But the still-new brain trust in Colorado needs to show it has real ideas about who will and who will not be able to function from the pitcher's mound in the Rockies' home venue.

Martin has real remaining upside, but Castillo is really the intriguing part here because he's a veteran with a lot to prove given the lack of long-term certainty around his contract status. Maybe he's done. Fine. It's only money, right? And you've still got Martin. But if Castillo flourishes by whatever definition that means when pitching in Coors, it's more than a productive performance for a team likely to land once again in the NL West cellar. It's a proof of concept. The Rockies need all of those they can get. -- Doolittle

Twins bring Gray back to Minnesota
The deal: Two years, $55 million

Grade: B+

Sonny Gray had one of the best seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins back in 2023, when he made 32 starts, posted a 2.79 ERA and a 5.6 WAR, and finished second in the Cy Young Award voting. (He won just eight games, plagued by a lack of run support and a poor bullpen.) The Twins are hoping for a happy reunion, signing Gray to the largest total value free agent pitcher contract in franchise history (tied with a four-year deal for Ervin Santana back in 2015). The second year is a player option, so this could end up being a one-year deal.

This wasn't necessarily where everyone expected Gray to land, especially coming off a strong season with the Boston Red Sox. He finished 18-5, tied with Cristopher Sanchez for the major league lead in wins, while posting a 2.72 ERA, good for eighth in the majors. While Gray had some injuries earlier in his career, he has been durable across the past four seasons, averaging 30 starts and 175 innings. That almost makes him Old Hoss Radbourn in today's game. While Gray's ERA has jumped all over the place, his FIP (fielding independent pitching) speaks to more consistency, with marks of 3.40, 2.83, 3.12, 3.39 and 3.47 going back to 2022.

The negatives: Gray is 37 years old and his strikeout rate took a big dip in 2026, dropping from 28.4% over the previous two seasons to 21.8%. That's still playable -- the MLB average for starting pitchers was 21.9% -- but it's something to watch. However, he's such a smart pitcher -- mixing in six different pitches with excellent command -- that he can succeed even with a lower K rate.

It's a nice move for the Twins, who ranked 22nd in rotation ERA this past season. They've indicated an intent to keep Joe Ryan. Plus, Pablo Lopez is aiming to be ready by Opening Day in his return from Tommy John surgery, so Minnesota could roll out a rotation of Gray, Ryan, Lopez, Taj Bradley (their top starter in 2026 with 4.4 WAR) and Bailey Ober, with Dean Kremer, Connor Prielipp and Zebby Matthews as depth. Ryan, Lopez, Ober and Kremer are all in the final years of their deals, so there are trade possibilities here, especially since Minnesota needs to improve the bullpen.

Gray's contract projection was for two years and $42 million, so the deal comes in higher than that; this might be par for the course for starting pitchers given Dustin May's inflated three-year, $52.5 million deal with the Chicago White Sox. In one sense, the best-case scenario for the Twins is if Gray has another good season and he opts out. If he does have a good season and Lopez bounces back, this has a chance to be a really nice rotation, with Prielipp having breakout potential in his second year. And a good rotation in the American League Central will make the Twins contenders. -- Schoenfield

Mariners add Garcia to infield in six-player swap

Seattle Mariners get:

IF Maikel Garcia

RHP James McArthur

RHP L.P. Langevin

Kansas City Royals get:

RHP Bryce Miller

RHP Logan Evans

LHP Jose Ferrer

Mariners grade: A-

Garcia is the best player in the deal, and the difference is enough to make this a slam dunk win for Seattle. Nagging injuries undermined Garcia's 2026 season after his breakout the year before; but even so, his contract and patience at the plate remained well above average, and he was still one of baseball's top defensive third basemen. While the injuries cost him in the power department and on the bases, Garcia is entering his age-27 season as a good bet to bounce back to All-Star form. His well-documented penchant for self-improvement also supports the argument for positive regression.

Under contract through 2031 on team-friendly terms, Garcia is a major upgrade at a soft spot on the Mariners' depth chart. Seattle's defensive projection at the hot corner leaped from 21st to first in my system, and the offensive leap in runs from that spot was about 10 spots, to No. 12. Garcia's range will only help the overall infield defense, as he will team with Colt Emerson, Cole Young and Josh Naylor to give Seattle a pretty dynamic group.

The Mariners had the kind of surplus on their organizational rotation chart to easily absorb the loss of Miller. Similar to last year, they look a little thin in bullpen lefties, but Ferrer didn't prove to be the splash addition in that role Seattle hoped for anyway. McArthur is a sneaky get here. He hasn't pitched in the majors since 2024 because of injury but was closing games for the Royals before getting hurt. He's a worthy flier. Langevin is a lower-level prospect, a righty with big strikeout rates and shaky command.

The Mariners' right-now win projection climbs over 90 with this trade, and at 67% division title odds, Seattle is a heavy early favorite in a soft division. This trade only bolsters the chances that the Mariners bounce back in 2027 to become the team we thought they were in 2026.

Royals grade: C-

The Royals just don't have the kind of organizational depth to be trading one of their few difference-makers for a package of pitchers who in total upgrade their staff only marginally and offer little collective upside. In the near term, the trade makes the Royals worse, and the problems only compound from here given that they had Garcia under team control for so long.

Miller moves right into a middle-of-the-rotation slot for the Royals, and if Michael Wacha declines, it's possible Miller will be Kansas City's top starter next season. Still, Miller, 27, has a career ERA+ of 95 and is at 80 over the past two seasons, both of which have been undermined by injury. For the Royals, the hope would be that Miller is ready to take the kind of leap that Wacha and Seth Lugo did when they joined the Royals. And to be fair, Miller's Statcast metrics definitely suggest that could happen.

Ferrer, as mentioned, had a poor season in Seattle after being acquired for catcher Harry Ford. Ferrer has a career OPS+ of 96 but still becomes the Royals' top bullpen lefty, almost by default. Evans was a ranked organizational prospect in Seattle and had a decent debut season in 2025. He underwent Tommy John surgery, the internal brace version, in January. He projected with mid- to lower-rotation upside before getting hurt.

The instant change in the Royals' projection kind of tells the story. The new pitchers are pushing not-great pitchers down the depth chart, so Kansas City's profile improves by about 16 runs on the prevention side. Garcia's defensive loss is fairly marginal for Kansas City, as Nick Loftin is a good defender, as well. But the loss of the bat is about a 17-run hit for the Royals' run production.

The end result? The same amount of bad, just shaped differently. The Royals should have received more for a player of Garcia's ability and contract. -- Doolittle

White Sox add midrotation piece with May
The deal: Three years, $52.5 million

Grade: D+

We've had two significant signings off the free agent market so far, and both involve freshly minted ex-Milwaukee Brewers: After Jake Bauers landed with the Boston Red Sox on Friday, the Chicago White Sox plucked Dustin May off the championship Milwaukee pitching staff.

Whereas Boston was banking on Bauers' 2026 breakout being his current true talent level, the White Sox are perhaps taking a bigger gamble that May's past five years do not represent his real level of ability. Since his early shine as a top Los Angeles Dodgers prospect, which included some promising early work in the majors, May's career has been journeyman-like. Around injuries that cost him the 2024 season, he has put up 0.9 bWAR with a 91 ERA+ over 356 big-league innings for the period covering 2022 through last season.

May became a fallback addition for the Brewers at the 2026 trade deadline after more glitzy pursuits (ahem, Tarik Skubal) fell short. May put up a 106 ERA+ for the St. Louis Cardinals before the trade and, given the Brewers' track record with acquired pitchers, you had to figure the move boded well for an even better post-trade performance. But that's not what happened. May had a 5.65 ERA and 75 ERA+ over 10 starts for the Brewers and was not a core part of Milwaukee's postseason rotation.

This uninspiring platform performance partially explains the grade above, but only partially. We'll see how things shake out in the market when we have more signings to work from -- May is the first pitcher to land a sizable deal -- but this seems like an overpay at least in terms of years. ESPN's Kiley McDaniel projected a one-year, $14 million deal for May, while a consensus projection from various outlets looked something more like two years, $24.7 million.

The White Sox are likely banking on May's tantalizing tracking data, which in 2026 had him in the 85th percentile in fastball velocity (average of 96.8 mph) and 72nd percentile in extension. Indeed, my own projection model sees enough in May keeping his value that it suggested a three-year, $45.9 million deal would be justified, which at least is in the neighborhood of what he got from the White Sox.

As it stands, May slots in behind Grant Taylor in the revamped Chicago rotation, just ahead of Sean Burke and Luis Castillo. Ah, Castillo: Is he a cautionary tale for a White Sox approach that liked him, as it likes May, despite underwhelming results before the deal? We'll see. May is also pushing pitchers such as David Sandlin and Davis Martin down in the pecking order, though there's no guarantee he's going to be that much better than them, if at all. I've got May adding 0.9 wins to Chicago's right-now roster, which pushes its 2027 playoff odds up by about three percentage points.

That's fairly marginal when you remember that the White Sox were overachievers in 2026. It was a great story, but it also means their starting baseline is somewhere south of the 84 games they won in 2026. If they are really looking to bolster their chances heading into 2027 -- and beyond -- then opportunity cost comes into play even though the White Sox should have some remaining spending capacity, or at least you would hope so. Would a little patience have netted them someone like Sonny Gray, Michael King or Freddy Peralta?

If the White Sox still go after someone like that and the May signing doesn't end up as their one big rotation splash, then maybe we push that grade up to the C-minus range. Given what we know at the moment, though, I'm underwhelmed. -- Doolittle

Red Sox get offensive boost with Bauers addition

The deal: Four years, $58 million

Grade: A

The Red Sox weren't high on anybody's list of teams likely to sign Jake Bauers given they already have an All-Star first baseman in Willson Contreras, but this signing is an early candidate for best move of the offseason. The grade reflects two thoughts: (1) that Bauers' breakout -- he finished 11th in the majors in OPS and third in on-base percentage this past season -- is for real; and (2) that the contract is a steal at $14.5 million per year.

Bauers will be entering his age-31 season, and, of course, spent years struggling in the majors before finally figuring things out, so while there would generally be concern that his 2026 season was a fluke, all the advanced metrics suggest the opposite. His Statcast numbers: 93rd percentile bat speed, 94th percentile hard-hit rate, 93rd percentile chase rate, 98th percentile walk rate. Those are real skills that aren't going to diminish overnight and should allow him to remain a productive hitter (he even hit left-handers well, so should project as a full-time player). Everyone saw the quality of his at-bats during the postseason throughout the Milwaukee Brewers' title run; he was named MVP of the National League Championship Series.

As for the contract, compare it to Josh Naylor's deal last year, when he signed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with the Seattle Mariners. Naylor was two years younger, but he was coming off a 129-OPS+, 3.0-WAR season compared with Bauers' 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR. Yes, Naylor had the longer track record of success but less power and a lower OBP. Signing Bauers for $58 million looks like a potential bargain.

Contreras is under contract for 2027 with a team option for 2028 and is the better fielder, so Bauers slots in as the DH. That leaves Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu in the outfield. Masataka Yoshida is still around for one more year as a backup, and the Red Sox will likely look to trade Jarren Duran, who still has two years of team control but is estimated to make $11.1 million in arbitration. With Duran coming off a bad season at the plate, the Red Sox might non-tender him if they can't trade him.

No doubt there will be criticism that the Red Sox needed a right-handed batter instead, but they actually had a slightly higher OPS against left-handers (.734 to .710). They just needed a good hitter, regardless of which side of the plate he stands on.

Remember that they also acquired the right-handed Curtis Mead from the Washington Nationals only to see him get injured in his first game with them. He'll be back and should slot in at second base. Boston also has shortstop Franklin Arias, one of the top three or four prospects in the minors who demolished Double- and Triple-A this year. Indeed, if Bauers comes close to his 2026 numbers and Anthony hits like everyone thought he was going to in 2026, this could be one of the best lineups in the league:

LF Anthony (L)

RF Abreu (L)

1B Contreras (R)

DH Bauers (L)

CF Rafaela (R)

2B Mead (R)

C Adley Rutschman (S)

SS Arias (R) / Trevor Story (R)

3B Caleb Durbin (R)

As for the Brewers, it's sad to see a postseason hero go, although not necessarily unexpected. They could have afforded this contract, but they have first-base prospects just about ready in Andrew Fischer, who led the minors with 48 home runs, and Blake Burke, who hit 34 home runs and stole 29 bases. They also have Andrew Vaughn on hand as a placeholder if Fischer and Burke aren't ready. Plus, they might need this money to sign William Contreras to a long-term extension. The Brewers will be fine. -- Schoenfield

Braves bolster bullpen by landing Phillips
The deal: Three years, $35 million

Grade: B-

The Atlanta Braves don't go after the biggest free agents -- B.J. Upton's $75 million deal in 2013 remains the largest free agent contract in franchise history -- but president of baseball operations Alex Anthopoulos does like to strike as early as possible in the offseason, and he did that again with Evan Phillips.

Phillips will essentially take the roster spot of Raisel Iglesias, so the Braves will get a little younger and maybe a little better, although Iglesias had a good season as the closer in 2026 following some bumps in 2025. The Braves had one of the best bullpens in the majors this past year, leading in win probability added while ranking fourth in ERA and sixth in OPS allowed. Iglesias departs as a free agent, but Didier Fuentes or Robert Suarez can replace him as the ninth-inning guy, with Phillips likely slotting in as a setup man alongside lefties Dylan Lee and Dylan Dodd.

Phillips was one of the best relievers in the majors with the Dodgers in 2022-23 before suffering shoulder and elbow injuries at the end of the 2024 season and finally undergoing Tommy John surgery in June 2025. He returned to make 31 appearances with the Dodgers in 2026, finishing with 33 strikeouts and just six walks in 26 innings. The stuff looked good -- he was throwing a little harder than pre-injury -- although he did serve up five home runs, and his injury history makes a three-year deal a little risky.

The belief was that the Braves' pitching priority this offseason would be a starter, but signing Phillips will allow them to stretch out Fuentes as a starter in spring training. He does have a three-pitch arsenal in his fastball, slider and splitter, and he has thrown a curveball in the past, so as effective as Fuentes was in relief as a rookie in 2026, it makes sense to see if it can work out for him in the rotation. -- Schoenfield

Tigers kick off free agency with Pagan deal

The deal: One year, $11.5 million

Grade: C

A key reason the Detroit Tigers finished 76-86 despite a plus-71 run differential was the bullpen: Despite finishing 12th in ERA, it ranked 26th in win probability added, so it performed worse in high-leverage situations. Out with Kenley Jansen, in with Emilio Pagan, who has been the Reds' closer the past two seasons.

Jansen was only 22-for-28 in saves in 2026, so maybe Pagan is only a small upgrade, but like Jansen, Pagan has been prone to the home run, serving up 17 in 111⅓ innings over the past two seasons. The Tigers are betting that getting out of Cincinnati -- where he allowed 12 of those 17 home runs -- will help. Pagan is a three-pitch reliever, with a splitter that he throws primarily to left-handers and a cutter he throws to right-handers. But his 95 mph fastball is rather pedestrian for a modern closer, and batters have hit 12 home runs off it the past two seasons.

Pagan is also turning 36 years old and his fastball velo dropped from 95.8 mph in 2025 to 94.9 in 2026, so there are a couple of red flags here. The Tigers had to add somebody to the bullpen, and doing so before the anticipated lockout is logical, but Pagan projects as a midtier closer rather than the elite guy Detroit needs. Kyle Finnegan and Will Vest both struggled in 2026, so the Tigers could still nab a reliable right-handed setup guy. -- Schoenfield

stories.headline: 'No one saw it coming': Inside the Swans' draft heist that landed a Lions Academy star
stories.summary: The Swans are notorious for bidding on draft night. But no one saw their heist of Lions Academy star Caylen Murray coming, given they didn't even meet his family. Jasper Chellappah looks into the fascinating happenings on night one of the AFL Draft.
stories.body:
Caylen Murray is the earliest pick to have his club-tied matching rights passed up in AFL Draft history. No one saw it coming, not even the Lions.

Make no mistake, this was a Sydney draft heist months in the making. The Swans ran the numbers and it showed Brisbane was three misly points short of matching a bid at pick 9. They pulled the trigger and watched on for five agonising minutes as trade partners disappeared one by one.

The three-time premiers were scrambling and the scenes unfolding inside their corporate box were increasingly uncomfortable. Each phone call was shorter than the last as candidates dried up in a race against time to find three points.

Up until that stage Sydney had not shown serious interest in Murray. They surely wouldn't bid on him without any leaks of interest from their camp; they surely couldn't bid on him without meeting his family.

A smokescreen devised in pre-draft analysis and 12 months of assessing Murray's talents was pulled at the perfect time to rip him out of Queensland. They feigned disinterest and caught the Lions napping. No one saw it coming, not least Brisbane's war room.

'Bidney' has been up to these tricks before. They'd made 11 bids in 10 years prior to last night, including Brisbane's own prospect Sam Marshall. They nearly snared Adelaide's Max Michalanney with a similar ploy in 2022.

As the dust settles, it's clear to see the Lions were undone by new draft rules that they themselves necessitated.

In 2022 they used 34, 35, 38, 40, and 41 to match Will Ashcroft's bid at pick 2. In 2024 they used 40, 42, 43, and 46 to match Levi Ashcroft's bid at pick 5. In 2025 they used 22, 23, and 39 to match a bid at pick 6 for Dan Annable. They achieved similar results for first-round talents Jaspa Fletcher and Marshall.

Brisbane had played the system to perfection up until Thursday night. But new draft rules require clubs to find the points to match with a maximum of two draft picks. A new draft value index (DVI) inflated the worth of top 10 picks. And a new levy added a 20% tax to bids matched by grand finalists.

Brisbane was caught looking too far ahead by sliding pick 19 down to 24 and 34. The 1355-point value of pick 9 became 1626 points with the grand finalist loading. Brisbane's picks 24 and 25 were worth 1211 points and they could go into a maximum of 412 points deficit on their future first-rounder. Tallied up and they accounted for 1623 of the 1626 points required.

The AFL values that gap at 1/1000th of the worth of the 3000 points Dougie Cochrane was matched with.

Sydney pulled off a coup to rival footy's very best off-field drama in 2026.

Brisbane's shortcoming wasn't just to the Swans's benefit, either. Gustavo Teixeira landed in St Kilda's lap at pick 11, a genuine pick one chance throughout the season. The flow-on effect kept coming with Collingwood grabbing their top target in mad Pies fan Sam Gayfer. Without the bid being matched these clubs effectively moved up the draft order.

Murray's shock was plain to see as reality set in. But the star academy graduate quickly recovered to deliver an extremely mature interview.

"I didn't realise Sydney was that keen but [I'm] stoked to join the club. It's an amazing club, great players, great staff and I'm keen to explore Sydney.

"It was a bit of a shock at the start but now it's sunk in. I'm stoked to be a Swans player."

The classy and composed halfback looms as a natural replacement for departed All-Australian Nick Blakey.

stories.headline: Revisiting sports and pop culture from GTA V's launch
stories.summary: "Grand Theft Auto VI" was released Thursday following a 13-year wait since GTA V.
stories.body:
Peyton Manning was beginning a record-setting season. Joel Embiid had yet to play a college basketball game. And "Breaking Bad" hadn't reached its finale.

That was 4,812 days ago, when "Grand Theft Auto V" arrived on Sept. 17, 2013.

More than 13 years later, "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Thursday, with athletes and teams counting down to its release -- and looking back at how much has changed.

Houston Rockets center Steven Adams even quipped during media day that performances could be impacted by the game's release.

"So look at NFL, look at all the leagues and watch them plummet. Just for the month of November, performances are going to go down," Adams said.

Before finding out whether Adams' prediction holds up, here's a look at the sports and pop culture landscape when GTA V arrived -- Sept. 17, 2013.

Seattle and Denver were starting their Super Bowl runs

The NFL had just finished its second week and two squads were in the early stages of dominant campaigns: Seattle and Denver.

The Seahawks' defense proved to be its superpower, earning the "Legion of Boom" nickname. Seattle allowed 273.6 yards and 14.4 points per game, both the fewest in the regular season. The Broncos averaged a league-high 457.3 yards and 37.9 points per game, while Peyton Manning tossed an NFL record 5,477 yards plus 55 touchdowns.

Both teams would finish with 13-3 records, setting up a Super Bowl meeting in February 2014. Seattle would emerge victorious on the biggest stage after stifling Denver's offense in a 43-8 victory -- and the seeds of Super Bowl XLVIII were sprouting as GTA V was released.

Miami Heat looking to three-peat

The LeBron James, Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh Big Three were entering their fourth season as teammates following back-to-back titles.

Miami edged out the San Antonio Spurs in the 2013 NBA Finals, an instant classic. The Heat faced a series clinching defeat in Game 6 before Ray Allen's late 3-pointer sent it into overtime. The extra period ended in a Miami victory to force a Game 7, where it closed out another championship.

The Heat faced the Spurs in a rematch in 2014, and San Antonio got its revenge this time around. But, for two straight summers, Miami reigned supreme.

Five stars preparing to go one-and-done

The 2013 college basketball freshman class had its fair share of heavy hitters.

In March 2013, then-high schoolers Andrew Wiggins and Jabari Parker graced the cover of Slam Magazine with the headline "Young Money: The game's next superstars have arrived." Wiggins and Parker were No. 1 and 2, respectively, in the SC Next rankings, but they were far from the only top prospects.

Joel Embiid, Julius Randle and Aaron Gordon all featured in the top 10 of the rankings as five-star prospects. Each of them, alongside Wiggins and Parker, went one-and-done and were selected in the top 10 of the 2014 NBA draft. Other notable names in the 2013 high school class included twins Aaron and Andrew Harrison, Noah Vonleh and Wayne Selden.

'Breaking Bad' nears its end as 'Roar' rules the charts

One of the greatest TV shows of all time, the final season of "Breaking Bad" aired as GTA V came out.

Two days before its release, the iconic "Ozymandias" episode aired. Series creator Vince Gilligan said that the episode is the "best episode we ever have had or ever will have." It remains one of the highest-rated episodes of the series on IMDB with 9.5 stars.

Pop songs led the way on the Billboard Hot 100 the week GTA V came out. Katy Perry's "Roar" hit No. 1 on Sept. 16, 2013, at the time matching Rihanna for the most No. 1's in the chart's 21-year history at 10. It took six weeks for "Roar" to reach No. 1, then-the fastest No. 1 hit since Perry's "California Gurls" in 2010.

Slotted in at No. 2 was "Blurred Lines" by Robin Thicke featuring T.I. and Pharrell. That track spent 10 weeks on the top before being dethroned. Lorde's "Royals" was at No. 3, while Jay-Z and Justin Timberlake's "Holy Grail" sat at No. 4.

The rest of the songs on the charts' top 10 included: "Wake Me Up!" by Avicii, "Summertime Sadness" by Lana Del Rey vs. Cedric Gervais, "Applause" by Lady Gaga, "Hold On, We're Going Home" by Drake featuring Majid Jordan, "Safe And Sound" by Capital Cities and "Berzerk" by Eminem.

WNBA, MLB teams were building championship legacies

The Minnesota Lynx won their second WNBA championship in 2013, and it would mark the beginning of a dynasty. Minnesota won two more in 2015 and 2017, the latter of which made it four titles in seven seasons as the club also won in 2011. Hall of Famer Maya Moore played a key role in each of the four championships. In 2013, she averaged 20.9 points on 53% shooting in the playoffs.

MLB saw similar dominance in alternating years from the San Francisco Giants. San Francisco missed the postseason in 2013 after World Series titles in 2010 and 2012. Someone privy to a trend could've predicted that the Giants would win it again in 2014 -- which they did. San Francisco hasn't won a World Series since, however.

BCS era coming to a close

College athletics looked entirely different 13 years ago, to say the least.

One of the biggest changes in college football lies in the implementation of the playoff system. Previously, the sport used the BCS rankings for 16 years to determine which two teams would play in the national championship game. That system had its fair share of controversies and came to a close following the 2013 campaign.

Florida State and Auburn made sure the BCS era went out with a bang at the Rose Bowl. Facing a four-point deficit with 1:05 left, Heisman-winning quarterback Jameis Winston led the Seminoles down the field for a game-winning touchdown. Two plays later Florida State closed it out to win 34-31 and clinch its first national championship since 1999 in memorable fashion.

stories.headline: Kayla Harrison, Amanda Nunes reclaim leading roles in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Who do Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes replace in ESPN's P4P women's top 10?
stories.body:
Hello (again), Kayla Harrison and Amanda Nunes. Goodbye (for now), Valentina Shevchenko and Zhang Weili. The top of the ESPN women's MMA pound-for-pound rankings has a new look.

Harrison and Nunes, both of whom had been ineligible for the top 10 because of inactivity, returned over the weekend for a clash of elites at UFC 334. Harrison, defending her bantamweight championship for the first time after nearly a year and a half out of the cage while healing from surgery for herniated discs in her neck, scored a fourth-round submission of Nunes, who had been retired for nearly 3½ years. As a result, Harrison takes over the No. 1 ranking and Nunes, a former two-division champion and the consensus GOAT of women's MMA, is No. 2.

The former occupants of those spots, Shevchenko and Zhang, are newly ineligible for the rankings because it's been over a year since they have fought and they have nothing scheduled. Those two former champions drop out, and the rest of the women's top 10 remains the same.

In the men's rankings, UFC heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane moves up one spot to No. 7 on the strength of his decision win over Josh Hokit in their title bout at UFC 334.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Nov. 18. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Kayla Harrison

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 20-1

Last: W (Sub4) vs. Amanda Nunes, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Harrison stepped into the Octagon at UFC 334 already a reigning champion, but her submission win over Nunes was truly her crowning achievement. The backstory about their shared training gym history added drama to the buildup, but what mattered most about this matchup was that Harrison, who had voiced her goal to be the greatest ever in women's MMA, was facing the woman who has lived up to that standard. After choking out Nunes, what can Harrison do for an encore? Can any other woman in the sport give her a fight? Maybe it won't come to that. Harrison and Nunes both called for a rematch -- but at featherweight. That would lessen Harrison's burden in dealing with her toughest foe: the weigh-in scale.

2. Amanda Nunes

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 23-6

Last: L (Sub4) vs. Kayla Harrison, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Nunes' return from retirement did not go as she had hoped, but her failing was not so much about deteriorated physical abilities as it was about her ill-advised choice to venture too much into the grappling wheelhouse of Harrison, a two-time Olympic judo gold medalist. If Nunes gets the rematch both women are calling for, but this time at 145 pounds, that would seem to be to the advantage of Harrison, the bigger woman. But a redo would give Nunes another opportunity to lean into her own prodigious strength as a striker.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 13-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Virna Jandiroba, Nov. 7

Next: TBA

If Suarez was still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Loopy Godínez. Then she went on to beat another fellow top-10 strawweight, Jandiroba, sending a message to the division that Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

8. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

9. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

10. Jasmine Jasudavicius

UFC flyweight

Record: 16-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Erin Blanchfield, Oct. 17

Next: TBA

Jasudavicius was rising in the 125-pound division until being knocked out by Manon Fiorot last year, halting a five-fight winning streak. But she got back up and won two in a row, most recently an impressive grappling performance against Blanchfield, to reassert herself as a contender.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Virna Jandiroba.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Kayla Harrison; 2. Amanda Nunes; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Natalia Silva; 5. Tatiana Suarez; 6. Cris Cyborg; 7. Alexa Grasso; 8. Manon Fiorot; 9. Dakota Ditcheva; 10. Virna Jandiroba.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Harrison; 2. Cyborg; 3. Silva; 4. Nunes; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Jasmine Jasudavicius.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Harrison; 2. Nunes; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Suarez; 9. Ditcheva; 10. Jasudavicius.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 15-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Josh Hokit, Nov. 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ made his first defense against Hokit at UFC 334, winning a slugfest.

8. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

9. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: Tied for 8th

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.
